archetype.name: Bubble Team (goaltending-first)
archetype.definition: A St. Louis side with even 5-on-5 play, an elite penalty kill and a hot starting goalie, held to a .500 record by an offense that can't finish.

report.headline: Hofer and the penalty kill keep a goal-starved Blues team afloat
report.take:
St. Louis at 9-9-2 is roughly what its goal differential says it is. It sits 19th in Goal Diff / GP at -0.2, its Pts vs Goal Diff is a near-neutral -0.8, and the site has it 18th of 32. That is not a lucky team or an unlucky one. It is a coin flip that has worked out some real improvements on last year. The 5-on-5 shares are dead even: 50.4% of expected goals and 50% of shot attempts, against 49.3% and 48% a season ago. The goalies have gone from -7.2 GSAx last year to +3.5. The penalty kill has gone from 76.7% to 84.6%, eighth in the league.

The season splits cleanly into two months. In October the Blues went 7-7 while scoring 3.14 a game. In November they are 2-4 and scoring 1.83. Over the last 10 they average 2.0 goals, 0.75 below their season rate. Two of those were shutout losses at home, and four more were one-goal nights. The defense barely moved, allowing 2.8 a game against 2.95 for the season. This is an offensive slump, not a collapse, and the offense ranks 26th by goals a game.

The numbers hide how much of the competence rests on one goalie. Joel Hofer has a .921 save percentage and 8.2 GSAx in 15 starts, seventh on the goalie tab. Jordan Binnington is at .851 and -5.4 in his five, 66th of 71. The team allows 28.6 shots a game, 25th, so it leans on its goaltending more than the even shot-attempt share suggests. The blueline grades D+, and Philip Broberg (20th of 259 defensemen) carries it at 24.56 minutes a night. Cam Fowler and Colton Parayko each play over 20 minutes and rank 193rd and 178th.

The finishing is the part most likely to turn. Skaters are shooting 10% in all situations against a league 11.4%, and the 5-on-5 PDO is 98.2. Robert Thomas, who leads the forwards in ice time, has 3 goals on 25 shots. Mason McTavish has 7 on 53, and Dylan Holloway has 4 on 49. Jimmy Snuggerud, with 10 goals on 43 shots, is the only forward finishing at a real clip. Some of the scoring should come back. Hofer is probably also playing above his true level, and the kill sits well above last year's. The likeliest result is a team that stays near .500 and fights for a wild-card spot rather than pulling away.

strengths.title: Hofer is stealing goals
strengths.body: Hofer has saved 8.2 goals above expected in 15 starts with a .921 save percentage, enough to keep the team's combined GSAx positive despite Binnington's struggles. The group's all-situations save percentage of .904 ranks seventh and is the main reason a team that allows plenty of shots sits 12th in goals allowed a game. Some regression is likely, but he is the clear starter and the goaltending grade is B+.

strengths.title: A top-ten penalty kill
strengths.body: The kill is at 84.6%, eighth in the league and 7.2 points above the league average. Last season it ran 76.7%, so this is a big swing and likely runs a bit hot. Good goaltending props it up, but even a partial fade would still leave it above average.

strengths.title: Even 5-on-5 play, better than last year
strengths.body: The Blues are at 50.4% of 5-on-5 expected goals and 50% of shot attempts. That is ordinary, but it is a real step up from 49.3% and 48% a year ago, when they finished 26th on the site. Nothing here says the true talent is below .500.

concerns.title: The offense has gone cold
concerns.body: Scoring fell from 3.14 a game in October to 1.83 in November. The last 10 games averaged 2.0, with two shutout losses. The skaters are shooting 10%, 24th in the league, and the forwards' top-minute center has three goals. Much of this should rebound because the chance share is even, but this group grades C- and doesn't generate many shots, so the recovery may be modest.

concerns.title: Thin blueline, many shots against
concerns.body: The Blues allow 28.6 shots a game, 25th, above the league's 27.1. The D+ blueline outside Broberg is a big reason: three of the four most-used defensemen sit outside the top 130 on their tab. The structure relies on the goalie to clean things up, which is a fragile formula over 62 more games.

concerns.title: No safety net behind Hofer
concerns.body: Binnington has a .851 save percentage and -5.4 GSAx in five starts, and he ranks 66th of 71 goalies. Every night Hofer sits is a real step down. Any injury or heavy workload for Hofer would expose the shot volume immediately.

trend.note: A .500 October has turned into a 2-4 November, driven almost entirely by scoring drying up while the goals against held steady. The last five games went 2-2-1, so it is a sag, not a freefall.

weekAhead.headline: Two leaky goalies first, then New Jersey and Edmonton back-to-back
weekAhead.body:
The week opens with the best chance the slumping offense will get. Anaheim's goalies stop .865 of shots (31st), and its defense gives up the second-most production to forwards relative to expectation. Pittsburgh's save percentage is 25th at .882. If the Blues' 10% shooting is going to correct, the first two games are where it should show. The catch against Anaheim is its power play, the league's best at 35.2%, running into a St. Louis kill that ranks eighth.

The weekend is much harder: New Jersey and Edmonton at home on consecutive days. The Devils already beat the Blues 5-4 in overtime this month. They control play, with the second-most shots for and second-fewest against in the league, though their 66% penalty kill is a target. Edmonton is 16-3-3 but rides a league-best 106.3 all-situations PDO behind a 47.3% xGF share. It can be out-chanced, but it finishes like no one else. Splitting the week would be a fair result. Sweeping Anaheim and Pittsburgh would make it a good one.

keyMatchups.title: Cold shooters against weak goaltending
keyMatchups.body: Anaheim (.865) and Pittsburgh (.882) are two of the league's worst save-percentage teams, while St. Louis is shooting 10%. Holloway and McTavish have plenty of shots and little to show for them, and these are the games to cash in. If the Blues can't score here, the slump starts to look like a talent problem.

keyMatchups.title: Penalty kill against elite power plays
keyMatchups.body: Anaheim's power play leads the league at 35.2% and Edmonton's is third at 34.2%. The Blues' 84.6% kill has been a pillar, and this week tests it hardest. Staying out of the box matters more than usual.

keyMatchups.title: Weekend goalie split
keyMatchups.body: With New Jersey and Edmonton on back-to-back days, Hofer may not start both. Binnington's .851 against a Devils team that out-shoots everyone, or an Edmonton team shooting 15.6%, is the week's biggest risk.

weekAhead.watch: Whether the Blues score three or more against Anaheim and Pittsburgh: that tells you if November's scoring drop was bad luck or the real offense.

restOfSeason.body:
The pace says 37 wins, 82 points and a -16 differential, and that is a reasonable middle case, with forces pushing both ways. Shooting at 10% against a league 11.4%, with an even chance share, should lift the scoring back toward the October level. Hofer's .921 and the 84.6% kill, both well above where this club sat last season, are the most likely things to slip. A mild fade there plus a mild rebound up front nets out to roughly a .500 team.

That puts St. Louis on the wild-card bubble in a Central where it sits seventh. The upside is a team that finishes around 90 points if Hofer holds up and the forwards start converting. The downside is the low 80s if Hofer cools or misses time, given the blueline's shot volume and Binnington's start.
swingFactors: Penalty kill holding well above league average

confidence.note: Twenty games played; the chance shares are steady but the goaltending and kill numbers are likely running hot.
